youtube.title: Your Cat Most Likely Can't Taste Sugar 🐱 (Things Living In Your House #64)
youtube.description:
Why doesn't your cat care about sweets? In cats, one gene of the sweet taste receptor (Tas1r2) is broken, so cats most likely can't taste sugar; the one tiger and one cheetah the researchers tested had the same broken gene. In a small 2020 study, cats were more likely to approach an unfamiliar person who slow blinked at them.

#shorts #cats #catfacts #thingslivinginyourhouse #meatballmyths

Sources: Li et al. 2005, PLoS Genetics; Humphrey et al. 2020, Scientific Reports.

youtube.title: Your Dog's Guilty Look Tracked Scolding in a 14-Dog Test 🐶 (Things Living In Your House #65)
youtube.description:
Why does your dog look guilty? In a 2009 test of 14 dogs, owners told the dog not to eat a treat and left the room. The "guilty look" was no different whether or not the dog had eaten it. It showed up more when owners scolded, and the effect of scolding was stronger in dogs that had obeyed. In a 2015 study of 96 dogs, owners did no better than chance at telling from the greeting whether their dog had eaten the food. These studies test the look, not what dogs feel.

#shorts #dogs #dogfacts #thingslivinginyourhouse #meatballmyths

Sources: Horowitz 2009, Behavioural Processes; Ostojic, Tkalcic & Clayton 2015, Behavioural Processes.

youtube.title: Never Run From a Grizzly: It's as Fast as a Racehorse 🐻 (Would Meatball Survive? #3)
youtube.description:
Would you survive a grizzly bear? The U.S. National Park Service says bears can run as fast as a racehorse, uphill and down, and that they will chase fleeing animals like dogs do, so do not run. If a grizzly attacks, the Park Service says to play dead: flat on your stomach, hands clasped behind your neck, pack on. Alaska's bear-safety guide narrows that to a defensive bear that has knocked you down, and calls it rarely necessary. If the attack keeps going, or the bear stalked you then attacked or attacked in your tent, fight back. Per the Park Service, a black bear attack is different: do not play dead. The Park Service also says no single strategy works in every situation.

#shorts #grizzly #bears #wouldmeatballsurvive #meatballmyths

Sources: U.S. National Park Service (Staying Safe Around Bears); Glacier National Park (Bear Safety); Alaska Department of Fish and Game (Framework for Bear Safety Messages). General information, not safety training.

youtube.title: Your Cat Can Likely Tell Its Name: Under 1 in 10 Even Meowed 🐱 (Things Living In Your House #66)
youtube.description:
Does your cat know its name? In a 2019 study, a hidden speaker played four ordinary words and then the cat's own name. Cats that had settled down during the other words reacted more to their own name. More than half answered by moving their ears and heads; fewer than 10% meowed, moved their tail or took more than a step. Cats living in a cat cafe could not tell their own name from the names of the other cats there. The study did not test whether cats come when called.

#shorts #cats #catfacts #thingslivinginyourhouse #meatballmyths

Source: Saito, Shinozuka, Ito & Hasegawa 2019, Scientific Reports.

youtube.title: Your Dog's Tail May Wag More to Its Right When It Sees You 🐕 (Things Living In Your House #67)
youtube.description:
Which way does your dog's tail wag? A 2024 review in Biology Letters says wagging is lopsided: dogs lean the wag to their own right for things they like, such as their owner, and to their own left for things that make them pull back, such as an unfamiliar, dominant dog. In a 2013 study, dogs watching videos of a left-leaning wag had higher heart activity and acted more anxious than with a right-leaning wag. It is a lean, not a rule: wagging goes with good and bad excitement, and a robot-dog study did not fit the simple story. A wagging tail does not always mean a dog is friendly.

#shorts #dogs #dogfacts #thingslivinginyourhouse #meatballmyths

Sources: Leonetti et al. 2024, Biology Letters; Siniscalchi et al. 2013, Current Biology; Artelle et al. 2011, Laterality.
